flaw.ctx: You asked for TTL. The expiry test passes.
flaw.answer: Expired entries are **never removed**: Get returns -1 but leaves them in the map and list. They count toward capacity, so the next Put evicts a *live* LRU entry while the dead one stays. Keys that are never read again stay forever — unbounded growth in a long-running process.
flaw.fix: Remove on an expired read; prefer expired victims at eviction; add a bounded sweep (see LruTtlCache).

qa.a: O(1) average for lookup, insert, remove; O(n) worst case if many keys collide. Enumeration is O(n) and order is not guaranteed.

Separate chaining, but without node objects: an `int[] buckets` of indices into an `Entry[]` array, each entry carrying its hash, key, value and a `next` index. Colliding keys form a chain through `next`.

When the entries array is full it grows to a larger prime (about double) and every entry is rehashed into new buckets — O(n) for that insert, amortised O(1). Pre-size with the constructor capacity when you know n.
Removing does not shrink anything: freed slots go on a free list for reuse. `TrimExcess()` shrinks. A struct key that is large is copied into every entry.
O(1) `Remove(node)`, `AddFirst`, `RemoveLast` given a `LinkedListNode<T>` handle. Storing the handle in the dictionary avoids an O(n) search.
No. Concurrent `Remove`/`AddFirst` corrupts its pointers (R3 corrupted in 20/20 runs).

qa.q: What does a bounded Channel do when full?
qa.a: Depends on `FullMode`. `Wait`: `WriteAsync` waits, `TryWrite` returns false. `DropWrite/DropNewest/DropOldest`: drops and `TryWrite` returns **true** (R14).

qa.q: When Interlocked instead of a lock?
qa.a: A single-word update with no invariant tying it to other fields — counters. Two fields that must agree need a lock.
SemaphoreSlim can be awaited (`WaitAsync`) and counts beyond 1; it is not re-entrant and must be released in a `finally`.

Most operators (`Where`, `Select`, `OrderBy`) are deferred: nothing runs until enumeration. `ToList`, `ToArray`, `Count()`, `First`, `Sum` execute immediately. `OrderBy` is deferred but buffers everything when enumerated.
The whole pipeline runs twice — including any I/O behind the source. Materialise once with `ToList()` if you need it twice.
An enumerator per operator, plus delegate and closure allocations for captured variables. Negligible for setup code, measurable in a per-request hot path.

qa.q: When is an explicit loop better?
qa.a: Hot paths, early exit with complex state, mutating as you go, or when you need to state complexity exactly — R5 hid an O(n log n) sort per call inside one readable line.

learn.title: 1 · Problem
learn.md: Add hit, miss and eviction counters to an LRU cache, then — before running anything — predict the hit ratio for several workloads. Then measure, and explain any gap.

learn.title: 2 · Clarifications
learn.md:
- Read-through `GetOrLoad(key, load)`: a miss calls the source and inserts
- Counters for hits, misses, evictions; a `Stats` snapshot
- Predictions for: a cyclic scan larger than the cache, a working set that fits, uniform random, skewed (Zipf-like)

learn.title: 3 · Key insight
learn.md: The counters are trivial. The question is whether you can reason about LRU's behaviour without running it. The famous result: **a cyclic scan of capacity + 1 keys gets zero hits** — every key is evicted just before it is needed again. Uniform random over D keys gives about capacity/D. Skew is where LRU shines.

learn.title: 4 · Approach
learn.md: Wrap the existing `LruCache` rather than editing it — the counters are a separate concern. A readonly `CacheStats` record struct with a computed `HitRatio`.

learn.title: 5 · Why the approach works
learn.md:
- GetOrLoad: TryGet → hit++. Else miss++, load, and if full eviction++, then Put.
- Workloads are generators (`IEnumerable<int>`), seeded, so predictions are reproducible.

learn.title: 6 · Data structures
learn.md:
| Type | Why |
|---|---|
| LruCache<TKey,TValue> | Reused unchanged — the requirement change touches nothing in it |
| long counters | Plain fields single-threaded; `Interlocked` if read outside the lock |
| record struct CacheStats | An immutable snapshot, so a reader never sees hits from one moment and misses from another |

learn.title: 7 · C# implementation — walkthrough
learn.md:
- GetOrLoad: TryGet → hit++. Else miss++, load, and if full eviction++, then Put.
- Workloads are generators (`IEnumerable<int>`), seeded, so predictions are reproducible.

learn.title: 8 · Complexity
learn.md: O(1) per request; the simulation is O(requests).

learn.title: 9 · Edge cases
learn.md:
- Cyclic over 5 keys, capacity 4: **0 hits** in 1,000 requests (predicted, then confirmed).
- Cyclic over 5 keys, capacity 5: exactly 5 misses (cold), 0 evictions.
- Uniform over 1,000 keys, capacity 100: 9.8% measured vs 10% predicted.
- Skewed (s=1) over 1,000 keys, capacity 100: 57.8% — far above uniform.

learn.title: 11 · AI usage strategy
learn.md:
- Ask for the wrapper only: "Wrap this LruCache with hit/miss/eviction counters without modifying it."
- Do the predictions yourself first, out loud. Then ask the assistant to write the workload generators — and check its Zipf sampler (the CDF and the binary search are where it slips).
- If measurement disagrees with prediction, ask for two hypotheses, not a fix.

**Prompts for this question:**

- *Check my design — no code* — "I believe wrapping an unchanged LRU with hit/miss/eviction counters keeps the requirement change out of the cache itself, and a cyclic scan of capacity + 1 keys should get zero hits. Review my reasoning without giving me the implementation. What would break it?"
- *Review, do not rewrite* — "Review my implementation for correctness and edge cases. Do not rewrite the code. List problems most severe first, each with the input that triggers it."
- *Race conditions* — "Now review this implementation for race conditions if multiple threads call GetOrLoad and the counters concurrently. For each race, give the interleaving that breaks it. Then name the smallest synchronization boundary that preserves correctness. Do not write code yet."
- *Tests that expose bugs* — "Suggest tests that could expose bugs in my implementation: boundaries, duplicates, empty and invalid input, and concurrency where it applies. For each, say why the expected value is correct."
- *Complexity check* — "What is the time and space complexity of each public method as written? Do not claim a bound unless every step achieves it."
- *Requirement change* — "The requirement changed: Add static class Workloads with Cyclic(distinct, length), Uniform(distinct, length, seed), Skewed(distinct, length, seed) (Zipf-like, s = 1) returning IEnumerable<int>, and CacheStats Run(int capacity, IEnumerable<int> keys). List which members need to change and which do not, before writing any code."

learn.title: 12 · Common AI mistakes
learn.md:
- Counting an eviction when the key was already present (an update is not an eviction).
- An unseeded `Random` — the numbers change every run, so a prediction cannot be checked.
- Off-by-one in the Zipf CDF lookup (`~idx` handling from `BinarySearch`).
- Claiming "LRU is optimal" — it is not; Belady's algorithm is, and it needs the future.

**Verification exercise:** Memory leak — Expired entries are **never removed**: Get returns -1 but leaves them in the map and list. They count toward capacity, so the next Put evicts a *live* LRU entry while the dead one stays. Keys that are never read again stay forever — unbounded growth in a long-running process.

learn.title: 13 · Concurrency considerations
learn.md:
The counters ride inside the cache lock if there is one. The trap is a cheap "lock-free" read of three separate counters: you can observe hits from after a request and misses from before it. Take the snapshot under the same lock, or accept and say it is approximate.

**Level 3 — Concurrency**

- *A scraper reads the counters while requests run.* — Snapshot under the cache lock, or Interlocked.Read and accept approximation

learn.title: 14 · Scalability considerations
learn.md:
**Level 4 — Scale**

- *A nightly scan of every key.* — Flushes the hot set — scan-resistant policy or bypass

learn.title: 15 · Production considerations
learn.md:
- Export as metrics with the cache name as a label; the ratio is computed by the dashboard from counts, never stored.
- Track per-key-class ratios if one tenant's scan can wreck another's hits.

**Level 5 — Productionisation**

- *What do you alert on?* — Relative hit-ratio drop with request rate alongside

learn.title: 16 · Follow-up questions
learn.md:
- *Add counters.* — Wrap, do not edit. Snapshot record. Say what a hit ratio is *for*: it is the fraction of requests that do not touch the slow source.
- *Predict the ratios.* — Cyclic > capacity: 0. Fits: (n − distinct)/n. Uniform: ≈ capacity/distinct. Skewed: much higher — say why.
- *Make the counters thread-safe.* — Inside the cache lock if the cache has one. If a scraper reads them without the lock, `Interlocked.Increment` and `Interlocked.Read`.
- *A nightly batch job scans every key once. What happens?* — It flushes the hot set — LRU's weakness. Options: a scan-resistant policy (2Q, SLRU, W-TinyLFU as in Caffeine), or route batch reads around the cache.
- *What would you alert on?* — Hit-ratio drop relative to baseline, not an absolute number; eviction rate spike; source latency. A hit ratio without request rate is meaningless.

**Level 1 — Correctness**

- *What counts as an eviction — does an update?* — No; only inserting a new key into a full cache

**Level 2 — Complexity**

- *Cost of the counters?* — O(1); the simulator is O(requests)

stages.name: LRU with counters
stages.yours: Decide what each counter means. **Read-through**: a miss calls the loader once and inserts. Hits, misses, evictions — and an eviction is counted only when an insert pushes an entry out.
stages.ai: **Co-generate** GetOrLoad. The LRU part is either yours already or a fields-pasted request like the LRU question.
bad: Add hit and miss counters to an LRU cache.
Counters in Get and Put separately: a Put of an existing key counts as a miss, the loader is never called, evictions are not counted.
No loader, so a miss costs nothing — the point of the metric is gone
good: Implement GetOrLoad(key, load) in CountingLruCache below. On a hit: hits++ and return the cached value without calling load. On a miss: misses++, call load once, insert, and if the insert evicted an entry, evictions++. Stats returns new CacheStats(hits, misses, evictions). Single-threaded. Keep my fields. List your assumptions first. Show only GetOrLoad and Stats.
States the edge: **a hit never calls load**
"Single-threaded" keeps it small; you will say what changes with threads
stages.reply: Typical defect: **evictions counted on every miss** once the cache has ever been full — or the loader called on a hit as well.
validate: A hit must not call the loader — count loader calls in the test
No eviction while filling; the first one at capacity + 1
HitRatio with zero requests is 0, not NaN
stages.fix: Counter placement is one or two lines → **by hand**.
stages.say: "A miss is a trip to the slow thing behind the cache, so that is what I count — and a hit must never call it."
stages.require: Implement `CountingLruCache<TKey,TValue>`: `GetOrLoad(key, load)` and `Stats`. An update is not an eviction.
stages.say_iv: Implement an LRU cache with counters: hits, misses and evictions. It is read-through — on a miss it loads from a slow source.

stages.name: Predict, then measure
stages.yours: **Write the predictions first**, in the pad as comments: a cyclic scan of capacity+1 keys → **0 hits**; the working set fits → only cold misses; uniform over N keys with capacity C → about **C/N**; Zipf-skewed → far better than uniform.
stages.ai: **Delegate the generators** (boilerplate) — never the prediction. Asking the AI "what will the hit ratio be" hands over the one thing being scored.
bad: Generate some workloads and tell me the hit ratio.
It runs the numbers and narrates them. You learn the answer instead of showing you knew it.
It made the prediction for you
"Some workloads" — not the ones that teach anything
No seed, so runs are not repeatable
good: Write three generators as IEnumerable<int>: Cyclic(distinct, length) = 0..distinct-1 repeated; Uniform(distinct, length, seed) using new Random(seed); Skewed(distinct, length, seed) where key k has weight 1/(k+1), using a running-sum array and binary search. And Run(capacity, keys) that feeds them through CountingLruCache. No analysis — I will predict first. Keep my CountingLruCache unchanged. State the complexity of each generator. Show only the generators and Run.
Names the efficient technique for Skewed
stages.reply: Typical defect: Skewed draws with a **linear scan over the weights** per sample (O(distinct) each — slow at 200,000 draws), or `new Random()` without the seed.
validate: Skewed: running sums + binary search, not a scan per draw
Cyclic with distinct = capacity: zero evictions
Prediction vs measurement — explain any gap out loud
stages.fix: A missing seed or a slow Skewed → **a one-line follow-up** naming the fix ("use new Random(seed)", "binary search the running sums").
stages.say: "LRU's worst case is a scan one bigger than the cache: every key is evicted just before it is needed. That is why databases add scan resistance."
stages.require: Add `static class Workloads` with `Cyclic(distinct, length)`, `Uniform(distinct, length, seed)`, `Skewed(distinct, length, seed)` (Zipf-like, s = 1) returning `IEnumerable<int>`, and `CacheStats Run(int capacity, IEnumerable<int> keys)`.
